title: Numbers and first purchases

grammarPoints.rule: いち に さん よん ご ろく なな はち きゅう じゅう. Four and seven have two readings each — よん/し and なな/しち. Use よん and なな: they are the ones that never collide with anything, and native speakers reach for them first when counting things. A price is one of these numbers with えん — the yen — glued straight onto its end: ごえん is five yen.

examples.ja: なな はち きゅう じゅう

grammarPoints.rule: The rest of the line: ろく なな はち きゅう じゅう. Seven has a second reading しち, and you will hear it — but なな is what you say when counting things or reading a price, the same way you say よん and not し for four. じゅう is the hinge every larger number is built on, so it is worth over-learning now.

〜つ is the ALL-PURPOSE counter for things: ひとつ ふたつ みっつ よっつ いつつ. It works for objects when you don't know the specific counter, which as a beginner is most of the time. It stops at とお (10) — past that you use the plain numbers.

antiPattern.why: the 〜つ series uses its own readings — ひとつ, not いちつ

grammarPoints.rule: いくら asks the price: いくらですか = 'how much is it?'. The answer is a number + えん. Prices are the one place a beginner needs numbers immediately, so this is where the number line gets spent.

Two adjectives finish the shop exchange. たかい means expensive — and, of a thing, tall; やすい means cheap. Either one can be the whole predicate: これは たかい, politely これは たかいです. かね is the money itself, which is why かねが ない — 'there is no money' — is how you say you can't afford it.

examples.ja: これは たかいです。

antiPattern.why: an い-adjective is already a predicate — it takes です politely and never だ: これは たかいです.
